paragraphs: He was only twenty. His brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, and their eldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First of all, I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was not a fanatic and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic. I may as well give my full opinion from the start. He was simply an early lover of humanity. He took up the monastic life only because at that time it struck him, so to say, as the ideal escape for his soul, struggling out of the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. And it struck him that way because he thought he had found in it an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, to whom he became attached with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. But I do not deny that he was very strange even then, and had been so from his cradle. I have mentioned already, by the way, that although he lost his mother in his fourth year, he remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, “as though she stood living before me.” Such memories can last, as everyone knows, from even earlier, from the age of two. But they rarely stand out through a whole lifetime like spots of light in the darkness, like a corner torn out of a huge picture that has all faded and vanished except that fragment. That is how it was with him. He remembered one still summer evening, an open window, the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all); in a corner of the room the holy image, with a lighted lamp before it, and on her knees before the image his mother, sobbing hysterically with cries and moans, snatching him up in both arms, squeezing him close till it hurt, and praying for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms to the image as though to put him under the Mother’s protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother’s face at that moment. He used to say that it was frenzied, but beautiful, as he remembered it. But he rarely cared to speak of this memory to anyone. In childhood and youth he was by no means expansive, and in fact he talked little. This was not from shyness or a sullen unsociability; quite the contrary, it came from something different, a sort of inner preoccupation, entirely personal and unconcerned with other people, but so important to him that he seemed to forget others because of it. But he was fond of people. He seemed to put complete trust in people all his life, yet no one ever took him for a simpleton or a naïve person. There was something about him that made one feel at once (and it was so all his life afterwards) that he did not care to be a judge of others—that he would never take it upon himself to criticize and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, indeed, to accept everything without the least condemnation, though often grieving bitterly. So true was this that no one could surprise or frighten him, even in his earliest youth. He came at twenty to his father’s house, which was a very sink of filthy debauchery. Chaste and pure as he was, he simply withdrew in silence when it was unbearable to look on, but without the slightest sign of contempt or condemnation. His father had once been in a dependent position, and so was sensitive and quick to take offense. He met Alyosha at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn’t say much,” he used to say, “and he thinks the more.” But soon, within two weeks in fact, he took to embracing and kissing him terribly often, with drunken tears and sottish sentimentality. Yet he clearly felt a real and deep affection for him, such as he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and it had been so from his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, and they looked on him quite as their own child. Yet he came to that house at such a tender age that he could not have been acting from design or cunning in winning affection. So the gift of making himself loved, directly and without knowing it, was inborn in him, part of his very nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed just the kind of child who is distrusted, sometimes ridiculed, and even disliked by schoolmates. He was dreamy, for instance, and rather solitary. From his earliest childhood he liked to creep into a corner to read, and yet he was a general favorite the whole time he was at school. He was rarely playful or merry, but anyone could see at first glance that this was not from sullenness. On the contrary, he was bright and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his schoolmates. Perhaps because of this, he was never afraid of anyone, yet the boys understood at once that he was not proud of his fearlessness and seemed unaware that he was bold and courageous. He never resented an insult. An hour after the offense he might speak to the offender, or answer some question, with as trusting and open a look as though nothing had happened between them. And it was not that he seemed to have forgotten the affront or deliberately forgiven it. He simply did not regard it as an affront, and this completely conquered and captivated the boys. He had one trait that made all his schoolmates, from the bottom class to the top, want to mock him, not from malice but because it amused them. This trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He could not bear to hear certain words and certain conversations about women. There are “certain” words and conversations that, unhappily, cannot be eradicated in schools. Boys pure in mind and heart, almost children, like to talk among themselves, even aloud, about things, pictures, and images that even soldiers would sometimes hesitate to mention. More than that, much that soldiers have no knowledge or conception of is familiar to quite young children of our educated and upper classes. There is no moral depravity in it, no real corrupt cynicism inside, but there is the appearance of it, and among them it is often looked on as something refined, subtle, daring, and worth imitating. They saw Alyosha Karamazov put his fingers in his ears when they talked of “that.” Sometimes they would crowd round him, pull his hands away, and shout nastiness into both ears, while he struggled, slipped down to the floor, and tried to hide himself, without uttering one word of abuse, enduring their insults in silence. But in the end they left him alone and gave up taunting him with being a “regular girl.” What’s more, they came to look on it with compassion, as a weakness. He was always one of the best in the class, but was never first.

When Yefim Petrovitch died, Alyosha still had two years to complete at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow left almost immediately after his death for a long visit to Italy with her whole family, which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha went to live in the house of two distant relations of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies he had never seen before. On what terms he lived with them he did not know himself. It was very characteristic of him, in fact, that he never cared whose money he was living on. In that respect he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who struggled with poverty for his first two years at the university, supported himself by his own efforts, and had been bitterly conscious since childhood of living at his benefactor’s expense. But this strange trait in Alyosha’s character must not, I think, be judged too severely. With the slightest acquaintance with him, anyone would have seen that Alyosha was one of those youths, almost of the type of religious enthusiast, who, if they suddenly came into a large fortune, would not hesitate to give it away to anyone who asked, whether for good works or perhaps to a clever rogue. In general he seemed scarcely to know the value of money, not, of course, in a literal sense. When he was given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it, so that it was gone in a moment, or he kept it for weeks together, not knowing what to do with it.
In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very sensitive about money and middle-class honesty, gave the following verdict after getting to know Alyosha:

“Here is perhaps the one man in the world whom you could leave alone without a penny in the center of an unknown town of a million inhabitants, and he would come to no harm. He would not die of cold and hunger, because he would be fed and sheltered at once. And if he were not, he would find shelter for himself, and it would cost him no effort or humiliation. And sheltering him would be no burden; on the contrary, it would probably be seen as a pleasure.”

He did not finish his studies at the gymnasium. A year before the end of the course, he suddenly announced to the ladies that he was going to see his father about a plan that had occurred to him. They were sorry and unwilling to let him go. The journey was not an expensive one, and the ladies would not let him pawn his watch, a parting present from his benefactor’s family. They gave him plenty of money and even fitted him out with new clothes and linen. But he gave back half of the money, saying that he meant to travel third class. When he arrived in the town, he gave no answer to his father’s first question about why he had come before finishing his studies, and seemed, so they say, unusually thoughtful. It soon became clear that he was looking for his mother’s tomb. He more or less admitted at the time that this was the only purpose of his visit. But it can hardly have been the whole reason. It is more likely that he did not understand himself, and could not explain, what had suddenly risen in his soul and drawn him irresistibly onto a new path, unknown but inevitable. Fyodor Pavlovitch could not show him where his second wife was buried, for he had never visited her grave since he threw earth on her coffin, and over the years he had entirely forgotten where she lay.
